intro: This guide walks a Sunday school class, homeschool group or family through “A Retrospect (For Children)” in twelve weeks, one chapter a week. It tells the true story of Hudson Taylor, who learned to trust God for everything in England and then carried the good news of Jesus deep into China. It works for a small family around the table or a class of up to twenty, and is written for ages 6–12.

Each session takes about 30 minutes. Welcome everyone and say the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter aloud (5–7 minutes). Talk together using the chapter’s three questions (5–10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or your own (2 minutes).

To prepare, read the chapter yourself beforehand and have paper, pencils and crayons ready; several weeks need nothing at all. A few chapters have frightening moments, such as a dangerous illness, a storm near the rocks and a night alone among would-be robbers, so read them calmly, answer questions simply, and keep coming back to the book’s own point: God took care of Hudson every step of the way.

weeks.summary: Hudson, about fifteen and bored, picks a little Gospel booklet out of a basket in his father’s library, meaning to skip the “preachy bit.” The words “the finished work of Christ” bring Jesus’ cry “It is finished” to mind, and he understands that Jesus has already paid for all his sins, so he kneels down alone and gives his life to Jesus. The big idea: we can’t earn God’s love; Jesus has done everything, and we simply receive it as a gift.

memory_verse.text: For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God.

activity.title: A Gift Already Paid For
steps: Draw a big wrapped present with a bow on top.
Draw a gift tag and write “From: Jesus” and “To:” with your own name.
Across the present, write “It is finished” in bright letters.
Hold up your presents and say thank you to Jesus together for his gift.

weeks.summary: Far away, at the very time Hudson was reading, his mother felt she must pray for him; she locked her door and prayed for hours until she was sure God had heard, then began thanking him. When Hudson came to tell her his news, she already knew, and his sister Amelia had been praying for him every day too. The big idea: God hears every prayer, someone may be praying for us, and we can pray faithfully for the people we love.

activity.title: My Praying Hand
steps: Lay one hand flat on your paper and draw around it with a pencil.
On each finger, write or draw one person you will pray for this week, such as family, a friend or a teacher.
Colour the hand in and write “God listens” across the palm.
Take it home and pray for one finger’s person each day.

weeks.summary: Practising trust for China, Hudson has only one half-crown left when a poor man asks him to pray for his sick wife; finding the family hungry with a new baby, he gives them his last coin and walks home singing. Next morning a letter arrives with a pair of gloves and a coin worth four times as much. The big idea: we can never out-give God, so we can share cheerfully and trust our Father to look after us.

memory_verse.text: Give to him who asks you, and don’t turn away him who desires to borrow from you.

activity.title: The Coin That Came Back
steps: Draw a large round coin on your paper and write “1” in the middle.
Pass your coin to the person on your left, saying, “You can never out-give God.”
On the coin you receive, add three more coins around it so it becomes four times as many, and pass it back.
On the back of your own coin, draw one thing you could share with someone this week.

weeks.summary: Hudson decides not to remind his forgetful employer, a doctor, when his pay is due, but to ask God to remind him instead. Pay day passes, the doctor remembers but has just banked his spare money, and Hudson keeps praying, until late on Saturday night a rich patient turns up to pay a bill and the doctor hands the money to Hudson. The big idea: our Father already knows what we need, so we can bring it to him first and trust his timing.

memory_verse.text: Therefore don’t be like them, for your Father knows what things you need, before you ask him.

activity.title: Who Do I Ask First?
steps: Stand in a circle and explain the game: when the leader names a need, everyone points up to God as fast as they can.
The leader calls out needs, such as “I’ve lost my shoe,” “I’m scared of the dark” or “My friend is sad.”
After each one, ask the group who God might use to help, like a parent, teacher or friend.
Finish by saying the memory verse together with a finger pointing upward.

weeks.summary: While training as a doctor in London and living on brown bread and water, Hudson pricks his finger and catches a serious sickness; the senior doctor tells him, “You are a dead man.” His first thought is sadness that he might never reach China, and then a calm certainty that he has work to do there and will not die; two other men with the same sickness die, but Hudson recovers. Mention the two men simply and keep the focus where the chapter does, on God keeping Hudson. The big idea: God has a plan for our lives, and we are safe in his hands until it is finished.

memory_verse.text: I will not die, but live, and declare Yah’s works.

activity.title: The Road God Has for Me
steps: Draw a long winding road across your paper, from one corner to the other.
At the start, draw yourself as you are today.
Along the road, draw three things you hope God might lead you to do as you grow up.
Write “My life is in God’s hands” at the end of the road.

weeks.summary: Hudson sails for China after a sad goodbye to his mother, and a fierce gale traps the ship for twelve days, until one Sunday night the wind drives it almost onto the rocks. When the captain asks about his call to China, Hudson says he would rather be there, obeying God, than anywhere else, and soon the wind changes and they sail safely out of the bay. Keep the danger simple; the chapter’s focus is Hudson’s peace. The big idea: we can be at peace even in a storm when we know we are where God wants us, because he is Lord of the wind and the waves.

memory_verse.text: He makes the storm a calm, so that its waves are still.

activity.title: Storm and Calm
steps: Sit in a circle and practise being the storm: rub hands for rain, pat knees for wind, and stamp feet softly for thunder.
When the leader says “Storm!”, make the storm sounds together, getting louder.
When the leader calls, “The wind has changed!”, everyone stops at once and sits perfectly still.
In the quiet, whisper the memory verse together, then play once or twice more.

weeks.summary: Later on the voyage there is no wind at all, and a strong current drags the ship toward hidden rocks while the sailors try everything. Hudson says, “There is one thing we haven’t done yet,” and the four people on board who love God pray for a wind; while a grumpy officer is still sneering, the top sail begins to flutter and the ship sails safely away. The big idea: when we don’t know what to do, we should pray first, not last, because God loves to answer.

memory_verse.text: Call to me, and I will answer you, and will show you great things, and difficult, which you don’t know.

activity.title: Praying for a Wind
activity.materials: One sheet of paper per child
steps: Fold your paper in half to make a little sail and hold it up in front of you.
Get into groups of about four, like the four on Hudson’s ship.
In your group, take turns praying one short sentence for a real need, such as a sick person or someone who is worried.
After everyone says “Amen,” blow gently on your sails together and watch them flutter.

weeks.summary: In China, Hudson’s English clothes draw crowds who point, laugh and shout rude names, so he chooses to dress like the Chinese people and style his hair like theirs. Now people listen quietly and invite him home, and his friend Mr. Burns soon does the same. The big idea: love thinks of others first and is willing to give up comfort or pride so that people can feel welcome and hear about Jesus.

memory_verse.text: Each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.

activity.title: Getting to Know You
steps: Find a partner, ideally someone you don’t know well.
Ask each other three questions: your favourite colour, your favourite animal and something you love doing.
Fold your paper into a card and draw your partner’s three favourite things on the front.
Give your partner the card, and say thank you when you receive yours.

weeks.summary: Hudson’s servant runs off with all his luggage, and with nowhere to stay he lies down on the cold steps of a locked temple, his money under his head. Men creep close hoping to rob him, but Hudson tells them he trusts God as his Father and stays awake singing hymns, saying verses and praying until they wander off before morning. This chapter can feel scary for younger children, so reassure them that Hudson was kept safe all night. The big idea: God never leaves us, even in the dark.

memory_verse.text: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you, the LORD alone, make me live in safety.

activity.title: Stars in the Night
steps: Colour the top of your paper dark blue or black for the night sky, leaving a few spaces for stars.
Draw five big stars in the spaces.
In each star, write or draw something you can do when you feel afraid, like singing, saying a verse or praying.
Write “God is always near” along the bottom, and keep it by your bed at home.

weeks.summary: Hudson learns that his own servant, a man he had prayed for, planned the theft of everything he owned in China, about forty pounds’ worth. Instead of having him punished, Hudson decides the man’s soul matters more than his things and writes him a kind letter urging him to be sorry and trust Jesus; later a friend in England, glad to hear of it, sends him exactly forty pounds. Forgiveness can be tender, so talk about everyday examples and keep any personal reflection private. The big idea: forgiving is hard and brave, but it is what Jesus did for us, and God takes care of those who forgive.

memory_verse.text: Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

activity.title: Overcome with Good
steps: Sit in a circle and explain: the leader will describe an everyday problem, and the group thinks of a good way to answer it.
The leader reads small situations, such as “Someone knocks over your tower,” “A friend takes the last turn” or “Someone calls you a name.”
After each one, let children suggest a kind, good response, and everyone gives a thumbs-up for the best ideas.
Finish by saying the memory verse together, quietly asking God to help you forgive.

weeks.summary: In Ningpo, Hudson and Mr. Jones feed about seventy poor people every day, with two signs on their wall: “The Lord has helped us all the way” and “The Lord will provide.” Down to one tiny coin, they set out to sell their stove but find the bridge washed away, so they go home, drink a little cocoa, and while they are still praying a letter arrives from England with money. The big idea: God gives us what we need for today, not too early and not too late, so we can trust him one day at a time.

memory_verse.text: My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

activity.title: Two Signs for the Wall
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half.
On one half, write “The Lord has helped us all the way” and draw something good God has already given you.
On the other half, write “The Lord will provide” and draw something you are trusting God for.
Take it home and hang it on a wall, just as Hudson and Mr. Jones did.

weeks.summary: Back in England, tired and unwell, Hudson looks at a big map of China and grieves for the millions inland who have never heard of Jesus, yet fears asking God for workers he would have to look after. One Sunday in Brighton he walks out onto the beach, gives the whole job to God, and boldly asks for twenty-four workers, writing the prayer in the margin of his Bible; peace fills his heart, and it is the beginning of a mission that sends hundreds of workers into China. The big idea: when we hand our biggest worries to God, he gives us peace and can do more than we dream, so we can ask him for big things.

memory_verse.text: Pray therefore that the Lord of the harvest will send forth laborers into his harvest.

activity.title: A Bold Prayer in the Margin
activity.materials: A large sheet of paper and crayons
steps: Draw a big rough map of the world in the middle of the large sheet, with China marked.
Around the map, draw or write places and people who still need to hear about Jesus.
In the margin around the edge, let each child write or draw one short, bold prayer, like Hudson wrote in his Bible.
Pray together for workers to go, then hang the sheet up where you meet.
